title: Future war in cities: Urbanization's challenge to strategic studies in the 21st century
thesis: Western militaries must engage with urban studies to develop nuanced strategies for diverse urban environments, moving beyond a narrow focus on megacities.
theme_1_justification: Not addressed. The paper does not discuss information goods, dual-use, or technology transfer between civilian and military domains.
theme_2_justification: Not addressed. No discussion of algorithmic opacity, epistemic authority, or surveillance as knowledge production.
theme_3_justification: Not addressed. The paper mentions smart cities briefly but does not conceptualize the city as a programmable system or discuss modulation.
theme_4_justification: Not addressed. The paper discusses urban warfare and civilian casualties but not spatial destruction, domicide, or home unmaking as deliberate strategies.
key_quotes: One of the continuing weaknesses of Western strategic studies is the paucity of serious research on the role of the city in armed conflict.
Because cities represent crucibles of civilization, it is uncomfortable to regard them as arenas for future armed conflict or as scenes of humanitarian emergency.

In the coming years, if we are to better understand the city as an armed conflict zone, an urban-oriented strand of strategic studies needs to be developed by security scholars working in close conjunction with the macro- and micro-level schools identified earlier.
policy_relevance: Recommends developing an urban-oriented strategic studies, engaging with urban specialists, and using discriminate force to reduce civilian casualties and uphold humanitarian law.
notes: The paper is a journal article focused on military strategy and urbanization. It does not address algorithmic governance, dual-use of technology, or the specific themes of the coding framework.
